extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers/students of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle's evaluative standards for moral character (virtues and vices) specifically for courage, self-mastery (temperance), liberality, prodigality, stinginess, and magnificence as described in Nicomachean Ethics Book IV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage (proper/true)
rubrics_metrics.description: True Courage: the disposition to face what is fearful (pain, death) with the right motive — from a sense of honour and in accordance with reason — rather than from compulsion, mere impulse, or ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle emphasizes that Courage is principally about withstanding painful or fearful things for the sake of what is honourable; it is a mean relative to us. The truly brave may still feel fear (even dread of death) but choose honour over safety. Courage is judged more by steadiness under sudden fear (showing fixed habit) than by anticipated danger. Anti-patterns: acting from compulsion, mere skill, animal spirit, anger, overconfidence, or ignorance do not constitute true courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage of Citizenship (honour/shame motive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bravery motivated by social honour and the avoidance of disgrace — acting because laws and social opinion punish cowardice and confer dignity on the brave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats this as the kind of courage 'most resembling' true Courage because it arises from a feeling of shame and desire for honour. Examples: Homeric characters (Diomed, Hector). Distinguish from true courage when motive is only social pressure rather than internalized moral choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage from Compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent bravery produced by external compulsion (orders, threats, physical coercion) rather than by an agent's own sense of honour or choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commanders who compel soldiers (by beatings, placing obstacles at rear, threats such as Hector's 'the teeth of dogs') produce obedience not genuine bravery. Such actions are lower than true Courage because the motivating aim is avoidance of pain rather than honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage from Experience and Skill
rubrics_metrics.description: A show of courage arising from familiarity, training, and technical skill in dangerous contexts (e.g., seasoned soldiers), rather than from moral choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates' slogan 'Courage was knowledge' is discussed: trained troops may repeatedly confront dangers of a kind they know and thus appear brave; but when danger exceeds their means they flee — exposing the difference from true Courage. Example: regular troops vs. militia at the Hermæum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage from Animal Spirit (impetuosity/ardour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boldness produced by strong animal impulses (ardour, rage, pain, lust) that drive one into danger without deliberative choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle notes Homeric phrases like 'infused strength into his spirit' to mark this impulsive state. While similar in outward effect, it lacks the moral deliberation of true Courage: wounded beasts, drunken men, or those goaded by lust/anger act thus and are not truly brave unless moral choice is added.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage of the Sanguine/Hopeful (overconfidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boldness rooted in confident expectation from past successes (or intoxication), not in a right estimate of the danger or moral choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such people are confident because they expect impunity; when expectations fail they flee. This resembles Courage in superficial confidence but is a deficient form because it depends on imagined invulnerability rather than virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage from Ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent bravery caused by not realizing the true danger; bravery evaporates once knowledge replaces ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Argives attacking Lacedaemonians thinking them Sicyonians — they flee when they learn the truth. Ignorance-based bravery is inferior because it lacks informed moral choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steadiness under Sudden Fear as a Measure of Courage
rubrics_metrics.description: A higher degree of Courage is shown by being undisturbed under sudden, unexpected fear than by facing foreseen danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle holds that steadiness under sudden fear indicates a fixed habit of Courage (less attributable to calculation), whereas foreseen dangers may be met by reasoning or preparation; thus sudden-fear endurance is a stronger proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage involves endurance of pain rather than pursuit of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage's proper object is resistance to pain/fear; it is praiseworthy because withholding oneself from painful or dangerous actions in service of honour is harder than abstaining from pleasant things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle compares to gymnastic athletes who endure blows for the pleasant end (crowns/honour). Even the fully virtuous person may feel fear of death more keenly yet choose honour; willingness to endure pain for honour is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfected Self-Mastery (temperance regarding pleasures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state concerning pleasures (mainly bodily pleasures of touch and taste): neither excessive indulgence nor insensitivity, but regulated desire according to right reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes mental pleasures (honour, learning) from bodily ones; perfect self-mastery concerns the latter (especially touch and taste). The self-master takes appropriate pleasures conducive to health and propriety, not in excess, not at improper times, and is not pained by their absence. He regulates desires by Reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of Self-Control (vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess with respect to bodily pleasures: indiscriminate or excessive desire for pleasant things, acting voluntarily on desire and thereby forming blameworthy habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This vice (unchastened-ness) is more voluntary and blameworthy than Cowardice because pleasure is an object of choice. Examples/labels: 'belly-mad', gluttons; likened to children in their grasping after what is pleasant. Habitual indulgence enlarges appetite and can expel reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience of the Appetitive Principle to Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The appetitive/desiring part of the soul should be obedient to and regulated by Reason; the self-master desires what Reason directs, in right manner and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses the metaphor of a child obeying an educator: appetites must be chastened. Perfected Self-Mastery equals the appetitive principle aiming at what is right, as Reason does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean regarding wealth: the Liberal person gives and receives wealth properly — giving to proper persons, in right proportion, at right times, from honourable motive, and with pleasure or without pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving is more characteristic of Liberality than forbearing to receive. Liberality is relative to one's means (proportionate generosity); the Liberal will also receive from right sources to have means to give, will not give to improper people, and will be vexed moderately if he spends unwisely. The liberal values wealth as means for helping others, not for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prodigality (excess)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive and wasteful expenditure of wealth: giving unrestrainedly (often to improper ends) and sometimes forgoing proper receipts; destroying one's substance through spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prodigality differs from Liberality because prodigals give not from honour but from unrestrained passions and often accept improper receipts to sustain spending. This vice can sometimes be corrected by habituation or change of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stinginess (defect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deficiency in giving and/or excess in receiving (base-gaining): close-fistedness, excessive carefulness about wealth, or receiving from improper sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stinginess appears in multiple forms: those who are sparing/close-fisted (deficient givers) and those who take base gains (brothel-keepers, usurers, robbers). Stinginess is common, more intractable, and judged a greater evil than prodigality because people incline toward hoarding rather than giving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtue of fitting large-scale expenditure: spending great sums on public/expensive works in a manner that is tasteful, proportionate to one's means and rank, and honourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnificence is like liberality but distinctive for scale and taste: the magnificent person seeks beauty and fitness in great works (temple furnishings, public spectacles, equipping a trireme) rather than minimal cost. Defect = meanness; excess = vulgar profusion or want of taste. The magnificent acts from honour and with pleasure, not from petty calculation.
